projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Jack Lloyd was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II veteran Jack William Lloyd. Mr. Lloyd served in the U.S. Army with the Third Armored Division. He served in the European theater and his highest rank was sergeant. I'm Tom Swope and this recording was made at Mr. Lloyd's home in Medina, Ohio on January 23rd, 2004. Jack was 80 at the time of this recording. Where were you living in 1941

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you have specific memories of December 7th, 1941?

sp.speaker: Jack Lloyd
sp.p: Yes, I do.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Tell me what you can about that?

sp.speaker: Jack Lloyd
sp.p: My brother and I were laying on the living room floor doing homework. My dad was listening to the radio, basketball game. My mother was sewing boat patches. She was very into that. The President of the United States interrupted the program and said Pearl Harbor--Harbor had been bombed and we now are at war with Japan.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your reaction when you heard the news?

sp.speaker: Jack Lloyd
sp.p: My brother and I looked at each other and we felt sure that we'd be engaged in a war and we'd be part of it. And my dad and mother, they felt the same way.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How old were you at that time?

sp.speaker: Jack Lloyd
sp.p: I was 15 years old at that time. My brother was a year and a half younger. And we were in high school.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember doing anything while you were still in high school for the war effort after the war began?

sp.speaker: Jack Lloyd
sp.p: Yes. As soon as I reached 17 I went to the National Tube Company, which made steel for the services. And they gave me a job working underneath the furnaces to keep all the scale clear of the units. And my brother went to a machine shop and he worked during the summers for the war effort, they called it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember much--dealing with much rationing and that sort of thing?

sp.speaker: Jack Lloyd
sp.p: The rationing hadn't really got into full swing before I went to the service. They were talking about it. Of course, I think they had some sort of food stamps on butter and tires and so forth. But I was at that age that I didn't realize it. Then we were on a farm so we didn't pay much attention to it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you follow the war news at all?

sp.speaker: Jack Lloyd
sp.p: Not really. We just never thought too much about it until our friends started to go. And some of 'em was enlisting and so forth and being drafted and then it started to hit home that we were going to have to join 'em, because we wanted to join 'em. So my brother, he was in the second year of high school and he turns 16. He was almost 17. He came home one night and he had some papers he wanted dad to sign allowing him to go in the Marines. Well, they talked about it, discussed it, and dad said, "Well, if you're going to go, you might as well go, something you want to do. You'll be drafted anyhow." So he signed the papers. My brother left for the Marines at 17 years old. My mother at that time told me, you're not going until you finish high school, I'm going to have one boy that goes--finishes school. I was, I guess, naive or whatever and I decided, well, I'll try it. Ten days after out of high school I left for the Army. I wanted to be a tail gunner on a bomber because I had a lot of friends that went to the Air Force. I passed the physical and everything and for any branch that I wanted to. I know a marine recruiter said, you're making a mistake. He said, "They'll lie to you." Well, at that time I took everybody's word. So they signed me up, said I'd be a tail gunner. And I weighed a hundred and 28 pounds and I felt that I could do that. That didn't happen.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Now, when you first went into basic training was it tough being thrown in with guys from all over the country? Was that a tough adjustment?

sp.speaker: Jack Lloyd
sp.p: I think the toughest adjustment was leaving home. They took us down to a railroad station. Was a very small one. There might have been a half a dozen of us from town. And they put us on a train. And seeing my dad and mother fade away as we went down the railroad tracks headin' toward New Jersey. And I'd just heard of New Jersey through school. I never been away from home at all. And the fact is we didn't travel much because during the depression and all we didn't have the money. So this farm boy was on the train with about 75 or 80 people in the car. And it was very silent ride up to New Jersey. Everybody had their own thoughts. And very few of us had ever been out--out of town. So it was--it was a mixed feeling. You goin' to serve your country and didn't know whether you was coming back or not to see your folks. It was--it was pretty scary. We got to Fort Dix, New Jersey. They kept us so busy there you didn't have time to get homesick. You was just thinking about when they was going to let you lay down or rest. They give us all kind of shots for different diseases and so on that we might encounter. They broke a needle off in my shoulder. I'm standing out on this porch holding my shoulder, leaning up agin a post. A sergeant came along and said, "What are you doing?" I told him my shoulder hurt, I just got a shot. He said, "I have a cure for that." Took me down to the kitchen and gave me a scrub brush and a bucket and says, scrub that floor and use that arm. I made about three passes with the brush and I threw the brush at him. I said, "I just can't do that." Well, you don't say can't. About that time a medical personnel come in. He said, "You just have a shot?" Yes, sir. So he checked my shoulder. He says, "Come with me, there's a needle broke off in there." So I went and they cut it out. I went back and this sergeant, he was still fuming. He said, "I'm not going to make you scrub the floor but," he said, "I got a roomful of potatoes you can pare." So I spent three or four hours doing that, and then assigned a different detail. So after about a week of testings, then they split us up into groups and sent me to Camp Pickett, Virginia, and for basic training. Now, it wasn't in the air corps because they said the schools was all filled up, there were too many people for that. So they said, you're going to be in a tank outfit. Well, I adapted pretty good. I thought, well, so what, you know, beats walking. The basic was a very simple thing for me because after lifting bales of hay and doing farm work, a little bit of walking around with a pack on your back was a piece of cake. And I really enjoyed it. It was sort of a comp--competition for me. And if you're in good shape when you go in and you do all the physicals that they want you to do, all the exercises, you'll be in better shape. And I think that's what brings you through. At least it helps. After basic training we went up to Camp Reynolds. They used to call it Camp Shenango. Around New Castle, Pennsylvania. That was a place where they gave you clothes. And if you were going to Europe they gave you ODs and suntans and so forth, heavy gear, overcoats. Now, if you're goin' to South Pacific they gave you mosquito netting and shorts. Well, first they gave me that and then he took it back and then they gave me winter clothes and so forth for Europe. That camp was only about 12 miles from my folks home, so they came up. And I had a little--another little brother and he was 12 years younger than me. So he was about six years old. So they came up. And we weren't allowed out of camp. So we'll go to the post movie. So they had a movie there and we went in. About halfway through the movie the lights came on and they start reading off outfits. If your named outfit was called you had to go to your quarters immediately. Well, mine was called. So I told mom and dad I'd see 'em around. And I knew we was going overseas. So my little brother, he kept saying, don't worry, he's coming back, he said he would, there's no problem. Well. I got on the truck. Put all our gear on it, which wasn't much. Clothes and so forth. They took us to Camp Shanks, New York. That was a port of debarkation. Well, we were allowed 12-hour passes. I met a fellow from Brooklyn that knew--knew New York pretty well, so I went on a pass with him. I can't say I learned a lot, but for a farm boy New York looked pretty large. I never saw such big buildings in my life. So up until that time--now, this is a big adventure for me. I had never been shot at and I never shot at anybody else. So this was really a--an adventure. Well, then they called our names, put us in trucks, took us down the Hudson Rivers and put us on a Liberty ship, 300 and some of us. Now, a Liberty ship isn't very big. And if you're ever taking a cruise, don't go on the North Atlantic in November. That was the most, most rough time I ever had. The waves were taller than most mountains in Pennsylvania. And this ship, as they called it, the propeller sometimes almost come out of the water. And then you'd go down in this valley and look up at the water. Well, fortunately I never got seasick. And there was very few of us that didn't. So I got candy rations and I was living pretty high. And I even volunteered to go to the crow's nest and watch out for submarines. While I was up there I asked this fellow that was in the Navy, I said, "How do you see a submarine at night?" I says, "Submarine's black, so's the water, and how--so how do you see 'em?" He say, "You watch for a white streak going through the water, and that's what it is." And he said, "Don't holler it's on the left side of the boat, holler it's on the port side. If it's on the right side, you say starboard." But, anyhow, I'm up there and the crow's nest would go out over the water and that, would come back, go out over the other side. Well, one night the destroyers came through our convoy, their sirens goin'. They're dropping ash cans. And that's 50 gallon barrels with TNT in it with time delays. Trying to disburse the submarines or sink 'em. I don't know whether any was sunk. I don't know whether we lost any ships or not, I couldn't tell. I didn't see any big balls of fire or anything. But to me that was still exciting. I don't know why, but it was. I guess because I hadn't seen anybody get hurt yet. And after 11 days of bouncing around we finally got to England.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was this crossing November of '43 or 44?

sp.speaker: Jack Lloyd
sp.p: In November.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Jack Lloyd
sp.p: So we got to England. They met us down at the docks with trucks. Took us to a little town of Warminster, which was about 40 or 50 miles from London. It used to be an old Army aircraft place that the British used prior to the war. And they left us use some facilities for tanks and half-tracks and for barracks and so forth. We stayed there from November till June. We went up to Wales and Scotland, Southhampton, and all over for maneuvers. And I still thought this was great. I don't know why, but I--it was an adventure to me. We'd go to Scotland and went down and saw the sea coast, flower gardens, mountains. Up in Wales it was flat country with green grass and off in a distance you could see towns. The towns had all trees surrounding the towns. And the Wales government wouldn't allow any U.S. troops or any other troops to go into their towns. They didn't want to--didn't want to socialize. But that was okay. So while we were on maneuvers in England we would shoot jackrabbits with .50 calibers. We didn't get any, but it was a lot of fun. One day in June of '43--or '44, they took us down to the beach. I call it a beach, it was right around--along the English Channel, and they start loading our vehicles into landing craft. Well, we knew we was getting close to something big but we still didn't realize what it was going to be like. We were still a bunch of young fellows. I looked into the channel standin' on the bank. Boy, it was as clear as a crystal. I could see little pebbles down there. It's pretty warm so I said, "I'm going to go for a swim." I take off my clothes. I got up on the bank and I run down there and I jumped in feet first, because I felt it was too shallow to take a dive. Well, I was wrong, I never touched bottom. And I came up and I was like I was paralyzed, I couldn't move. And if it hadn't been for the fellows making a human chain and pulling me back on the shore, I'd have drowned. That water was so cold it just paralyzed you. That's why the swimmers have to have special grease and suits and so on to swim in the Channel. And if you was to get--get out there and have your craft disabled, you wouldn't last too long. Well, finally they put us on these LCT, told us we was heading out. They still didn't tell us where we were goin'. Well, the voyage over there lasted about seven hours. I don't think there was a sound made on that landing craft. Nobody talked, nothing. Everybody had his own--own fears and apprehensions and so on. We finally got to Omaha Beach. Then all heck broke loose, and we knew why we were there. We finally got onto shore and I never seen so many people injured and killed and so forth in my life. And if--if somebody said they weren't afraid, they weren't there. That's a fact. We finally got on the beach and up into the hedgerows in France. And the water at night when we'd come back, the surf coming into the shore was tinted like pink. And it wasn't from dye, it was human sacrifices. And the bodies were piled up on both sides of this dirt road like cord wood for maybe a mile back into the hedgerows of France. Well, finally we had a lot of trouble trying to move our equipment because you couldn't get through the hedgerow. Now, a hedgerow is about six to eight feet high and about two feet thick made of stone and dirt. But through the years they'd grown and grass in there and trees and brush. We couldn't get through. The French used to believe that kept the evil spirits out of their crops. Well, it kept our tanks from movin' too. Maybe we were evil spirits, I don't know. Well, finally we got to Saint Lo. We couldn't take that town. The Germans had pulled back from the beach and set up heavy fortifications. So they called the air corps in from England. And they set it up. And one day they kept us about a quarter of a mile away up on a hill. And it was woods there and so forth and we had camouflage on our tanks and half-tracks. Here came the planes. Wave after wave after wave of bombers and fighters. They say there was over 2,000 of 'em came out of England. They bombed Saint Lo. We'd see some of our planes coming down, they'd been shot. Antiaircraft. The sky was black with flak. Finally, after the raid was over--and our clothes used to vibrate like you was standing in the wind from the concussion of those bombs. I couldn't imagine going through something like if I'd have been a German. Well, after the raid was over we was told to take Saint Lo. It was like driving over a--sand dunes from all the craters the bombs had left. And the Germans were staggering around like they'd been on dope or intoxicated from the concussion of those bombs, so they didn't put up much of a resistance. You get into Saint Lo. And just as we was entering town a woman was standing there with a dead baby over her one arm and giving us the victory sign. And to me, I was shook up bad. And I saw that and I was shook up worse. But they had women up on the balconies. They'd cut all their hair off and paintin' them red because they'd fraternized with the Germans. In retrospect, what else would you expect them to do? If you didn't do that, they'd either kill you or rape you, so you might as well try and adapt to the situation. We went through there. Then our first obstacle was the Siegfried line. That consisted of pyramids made out of steel and concrete. And they were staggered so we couldn't get tanks through. So at night the corps of engineers came in, put TNT on them and blew us a path through. Well, that was great. But we came to what they call pillboxes. They looked like igloos. They were made out of cement and steel and they were about three feet thick and about 15 feet or 20 in diameter. And they buried 'em in the ground and just left about four foot sticking out of the ground with gun slots in 'em. They had big guns in there. Well, you can't hardly knock one of 'em out. We weren't good enough or lucky enough to shoot 'em right in those slots. We lost a lot of tanks and men there. Air corps come in and tried to bomb them out, and that didn't work. So they finally got some people that volunteered to put flame throwers on their tanks. They went up there at night. And after a heavy cost they finally rousted the Germans out. Some of them come running out still on fire. For a farm boy that never saw any fights, only a little fistfight, this was very traumatizin'. We finally got through there and we went into Auchen, Germany. And almost every house there had a hole blown through it. The armored infantry would go through those holes and clean the Germans out of the houses. Well, we got into Stolberg, Germany. And it was in October of '44. Started to snow and sleet, rain, and the mud. So the tanks wasn't a good situation for 'em. It wasn't for the Germans either. So we held half the town of Stolberg and the Germans held the other half. And if they'd have had malls at that time, it wouldn't have been a good idea to go shopping. Well, all we did was patrol. And that's what the Germans did. But every night Bed Check Charlie would come, drop his flares and throw one bomb, 500 pounder, just to let 'em know they was there. That was a one-wing propellered plane. I call 'em piper cubs. Because at that time we didn't have jets. We didn't even know what a jet was. And this fellow would come every night and take pictures and so forth and then he'd drop his one bomb and leave. But once in a while they'd send in some Messerschmits. They'd fly so low that they'd hit the antennas on our tank. We weren't allowed to move, shoot, or anything. Just stay still. Because we had camouflage over the tanks. And I don't suppose their map showed an orchard. That's what we looked like from the air. But they didn't bomb or anything, they'd keep flying back and forth. You could even see the pilots in the cockpit looking. That was a little frightening. We always expected to have bombers come in afterwards, but we never did. One morning I was to go on patrol. The next day I was supposed to go to Paris for a ten-day furlough. I'd been on the front lines for six months and they felt like I needed a rest. Well, I felt like it too. But, anyhow, I had everything all lined up in my vehicle for the next day. Well, they came around and they said, you're going out on patrol. So we took a half-track and we started out. About ten o'clock in the morning I saw a flash off to one side. Then I heard a big noise. The next thing I remember I was on the ground, my side was hurting very bad, and I looked up and there was a German standing there kicking me in the ribs hollering "rasch" to get me up. I didn't know what "rasch" was, but I didn't like laying there being kicked either, so I got up. My left knee hurt, my right eardrum was blown out. But I got up. There was another fellow there. He wasn't hurt too bad either, so he got up. We had one fellow, his legs was pretty bad. So we reached over to help him out, and the Germans hit us in the back with a rifle butt and told us to get away from him, pushed us away. We got about 50 yards away, we heard a shot. That was their first aid. So we knew then we had a real problem. Because when we took prisoners we'd give 'em candy bars and cigarettes and shipped 'em on back away from the front lines. When they took prisoners, they didn't want 'em. Of course, it was towards the end of the war and they, I feel, knew they were losin', but they wouldn't admit it. They took us down to a limestone cave. They put us in there and one whole wall--this cave was about 50 foot in diameter. It wasn't very high. But they had bleachers on three walls and they had fresh troops sitting in there to relieve the front lines. The other wall was full of radios for communications. Well, the Germans that were on relief, they would spit at you, swear at you, push you, and all you could do is stand there and look at them. So just about dark they took us out of there and we went down to an old farm house in the valley. Well, on the way down our artillery plane thought we was a German patrol, so they brought the 155s and 105 Howitzers into play and almost killed us. We finally got into this house. They put us in the basement. The artillery barrage lasted for three or four hours. We came out after dark and the house was gone. All that was left is the floor and the basement. We were all dusty and dirty from the shelling. They put us in a--a car. It looked like a Volkswagon Beetle. They put he and I in the back and they had a guard in the front as a passenger and then they had the driver. I knew if we got any further away from the front lines we wouldn't have a chance of escape. So I told my buddy, I said, "You take care of him and I'll take care of the driver.". Well, the passenger raised a pistol up over the back seat and he said, "I wouldn't try that if I were you." He spoke better English than I did. So J. B. said, "What'll we do now?" And I said, "Nothing." I didn't even have a plan B and plan A didn't work at all. So we drove, I don't know, half an hour, an hour. They took us out of there. There was a cement block building about 20 by 20, no windows in it. It had a steel door, a cement floor. It was very damp in there. Water dripping off the ceiling. No heat, nothing. They put us in there and shut the door. We didn't know whether they was coming back or not. At that point I didn't care. I don't know how long we were in there, but it was a long time. They finally opened the door and the sunlight on the snow, just you couldn't see, so they'd help us along with rifle butts in the back. We walked about 12, 15 miles. Took us into a farm house. Was going to interrogate us. Well, I didn't really know that much, but I knew how many tanks and so forth, I could guess at 'em. But I wouldn't tell 'em. They asked me how many tanks was on the hill and half-tracks. I said, "I doubt if there's any. I only run one at a time, so I don't know" Well, I guess I had too much of that patriotism shot, I wouldn't tell them any difference. And so they took a pair of big leather gloves out. This officer got up and he slapped me around pretty good. They had another German with a bayonet right in my back. So he--and you better not even look nasty at the guy that was giving you a beating. So after he got tired of that he interrogated my buddy. My buddy, he was sort of a wise guy. He said, "Oh, I think we got a million or two up there." Well, they didn't like that answer either, so he got the same treatment I got. They took us in a back room. Take off all your clothes. Now, this is dead of winter and cold. One of the coldest ones they had recorded in years. There were no heat in this place. So we take our clothes off. They gave me a pair of wooden shoes, a pair of cotton pants, and a shirt, and I had one sleeve missing. That was my wardrobe. That was the only thing I was supposed to have till the end of the hostilities. We left there. And they marched us for I don't know how many hours. We finally got to a railroad station, or railroad yard in Hamburg, Germany. By that time I couldn't hardly walk, I hadn't had anything to eat in a couple of days, my back hurt very bad from being beat on. Plus my ear was startin' to get infected from the blown out eardrum. My left knee wasn't working too well. I couldn't get up into the car. There's about a three or four foot leap up there, I couldn't make it. They just picked me up bodily and threw me in. My buddy got in. I crawled over in a corner and sit down. There were 78 people in that car. They smelled very bad. I don't know how long they'd been in there. Well, a couple of guys from Oklahoma, one from Florida, put a coat over me. I don't know where they got it, but they put it over me. They said, he won't last till daylight. I heard 'em say that. I didn't think I was in that bad of shape, but I guess maybe I was. Looked worse than I was. Well, for 17 days every night we'd get bombed and strafed by our own planes. They didn't have these cars marked as prisoners of war so these planes didn't know any better and they bombed and strafed. Had a fellow--a fellow from Texas got up, and he started praying. Put his hands up in the air. He took a 20 millimeter in the chest. Well, you know, mornings after the raids the guards would open the door and tell us to throw out the dead and wounded. Well, the wounded would holler quite a bit when you start dragging 'em across the floor of the car. So we'd hit 'em in the head with a wooden shoe and then knock 'em out and then throw 'em out. After 17 days, when we pulled out of there that pile was still there, they hadn't even sorted 'em out. Needless to say, I made it. The first two or three days I guess was pretty crucial, but I made it. They'd feed you about every three days, if you needed it or not. Give you a slice of bread or a old cow bean. These cow beans tasted like cornstalks. Sometimes they cooked 'em and sometimes they didn't. Well, after the boxcar ride they took us out and started to walk. Well, they didn't have camps at that time. They were all filled with other prisoners. So the ones at the end of the war had this walking spell. They'd walk you around all over Germany, trying to keep you away from the American lines and try to keep you away from the Russian lines. And it was, like I say, cold. I hear people say they're cold now and I just sort of smile, because you don't know what cold is till you sleep out with no socks, no underclothes, just a pair of pants and a shirt, wooden shoes, you walk all day, drink green water out of a ditch, get fed a couple of times a week, and then lay out in the snow. We used to dig holes in the snow to keep the wind off of us. You'd wake up in the morning, you couldn't even open your eyes because your lashes will be frozen. The inside of that hole was just solid ice from condensation. There was a lot of people never got out of them holes. They died. People had appendicitis, pneumonia, any illness at all, you was done. There was no first aid. Even their own people. One woman came out. She was elderly. Her husband sittin' on the steps of this farm house. She come out with a tea kettle of hot water, was going to give us something to drink that was warm. The guard on horseback rode over and hit her in the mouth with a rifle butt and knocked her down. We weren't allowed to help her up or even stop to find out if she was okay. The last I remember, I looked around and her husband was sitting in the road with her head on her lap. So they treated their own people bad then too. Well, finally in about April--now, by now my hair was down around my shoulders and I guess I looked like a skinny Geronimo. But we got into April. They put us in a fence, barbwire, guards around, machine gun towers. And they had a big circus tent. They put us in there. Well, at least it kept the sleet and the snow off you. The ground wasn't snow. It was hard, cold, but at least it wasn't snow on it. One day it was sleeting very bad and they decided they're going to count us. We decided we wasn't going out and getting all wet and then have to go back in and take two or three days to dry out, so we didn't go out. They sent some Doberman pinschers in, six of 'em. They used silent whistles to command them. The dogs come into the tent and there was an awful commotion. It ended up they were two dogs short. Some of us got something to eat. So they didn't try that again. Well, along about the end of April a guy and I, we decided we're going to leave, we'd had enough of this. We could see flashes at night of our artillery in a distance. That's where we were going. We took the log they had across the latrine and we threw it up agin a fence in a rainstorm. And it was thundering and lightening and raining bad, the guards were in their little shanties. We decided this was the time. Crawled up that log and hopped over to the other side of the fence and took off. It was like the plains were a prairie. There wasn't a house or tree or anything. We didn't care, we was heading for the lights of our artillery. We got about a quarter of a mile away, the moon came out, it quit raining. Just like somebody shut it off. The moon started to come out from the clouds and that makes very good tracking weather for dogs. So we hear the dogs. The fellow said, "What are we gonna do?" I said, "We might as well stop and wait on them." So all we could see was prairie, no place to go. What we were gonna do is find a farm house, take their clothes and head out. We didn't get that far. The reason we didn't, I was about a hundred and 12 pounds. The only thing that was strong in me was a desire for freedom, and I thought my body was gonna follow along and do that. But we were out of condition and really weakened state. In retrospect, we shouldn't even have tried it. But, anyhow, they brought the dogs up. They had one old fellow--he may have been in the first World War--and they had two young fellows. They were in the S.S. troops. That's who guarded us. They gave--they brought the dogs up and left them get within three or four inches of your face, and they're standing on their hind legs. You can see teeth clear down their throat. They were growling really bad. Well, finally they pulled the dogs back and took 'em back and gave 'em to this old guy to hold. They threw up their rifles and started to count. Just as they get to a crucial number, the old fellow jumped in front of 'em and they had a big argument in German. Finally the young guys pushed him away. Again they threw up their rifles, they start counting again. And I'll give the old guy credit, he jumped in front of 'em again. They had another argument. So they just--two young fellows came around behind us, took their rifle butts and marched us back to camp. About every third step they'd give you a shot. That--when you're real skinny, that bone's pretty close to the skin. It hurt very bad. But they took us back and hung us on a barbwire fence. You'd have to reach up as high as you could and then they'd tie you off. The last thing I remember is my hands looking sort of between blue and black and swelled up like footballs. Maybe not quite that large, but they looked larger than normal. Then I--the next thing I remember, I woke up and I was in solitary confinement. What it was, looked like an old stone house underground where they used to store food, potatoes and so on. But it had a steel door on it, no light at all. I don't know how long I was there. I have no idea. They finally took us out and threw us back into camp. In May, the first part of May of '44 the Russians came. We saw the guards all nervous. Finally the Russians came through the fences and so on with the tanks. They had women on horseback. They had fur hats, high boots and sabers. They was running the guards down. That's when I decided I wouldn't marry a Russian. They were a little rough for me. Well, they had a little town down--a German town about a half a mile from camp. Now, we were supposedly to be free but the Russians wouldn't allow us to do anything. They did give us some food. We went down to this little town and all the _____ from the houses was sitting along the curb on both sides of the street. And I asked this fellow, I said, "What are they--what are they doing?" He said, "You got to see this." What they did, they had six young German soldiers standin' in the street, a Russian guarding them. The officer went up to each one of 'em and slapped 'em in the face with a pair of leather gloves. Rattle off something in Russian. And the Russian soldier would take his bayonet and then stab him in the rectum and run him down the street, run him back up, and then shot him. They did that with all six of 'em with the civilians sitting in the road chairs watching this. To me, that was the most barbaric thing I'd seen in a long time. So finally somebody got ahold of a radio, and they radioed our lines, said we'd just soon come back to the U.S. as stay with the Russians. Well, they sent a convoy of six trucks. Now, you can't get 300 people on six trucks. But we sort of wandered out of camp, so it wasn't conspicuous. And when the trucks came there was a mad rush to get on 'em. I don't know what happened, I guess I was lucky, I got on one. So we're going back to the--our lines. Came to a river. And this bridge, there were two Russian soldiers there. They had their rifles in port, wantin' us to stop. And the captain had a bullhorn and he said if they don't move, run over 'em. Well, right at the last minute the soldiers jumped aside and we went across the bridge. Now we were in U.S. hands, which we felt very relieved, because I still believe the Russians took a lot of 'em up to Siberia. Never heard of them again. And they was going to charge the United States a dollar apiece and ship us through Odessa and the Black Sea to turn us over to the Americans. Well, anyhow, we got back to the U.S. soldiers. The first thing they did was took all our clothes and burnt 'em, which was a good move. They had to put water on my wooden shoes to get 'em off my feet. I hadn't had 'em off for six months. Because once you took 'em off, your feet would swell up and you'd never get 'em back on. And although they weren't much use, they were better than bare feet. Then they took us, they sit--sit down on an orange crate. I sat down. They said, we're going to have a haircut, how do you want it? I said, "I don't care." Now, I might as well have said that because it didn't make any difference anyhow, they cut 'em all right down to the skull. Well, then they took us into the showers. That's the first shower we'd had in six months. We'd never had any showers, no toothbrush, combs, nothin'. Well, that felt great. I could've stayed there for a long time. You had your time limit. Came out of that and they sprayed powder on you. What that did was kill the lice. And then you felt lonesome for a while, because you was used to those little suckers. But, anyhow, they gave us some clothes. Half of 'em didn't fit, but I don't care, they was warm. And then they said there was planes coming to take us back to France to Camp Lucky Strike. They brought in C-47 cargo planes and landed 'em in a field. I got up to the door. A big sergeant says, "The plane's full, you have to wait for the next one." I said--I felt really relieved. I said, "I don't care, I got time." So that plane left. They brought in another plane and I got on it. And the first thing I did is go to sleep. I bet it wasn't in the air five minutes. That's the first time I felt safe for a year. Because I had six months in combat and six months at prison. So I went to sleep. We got to France. END OF FIRST FILE ON CD; BEGINNING OF SECOND FILE ON CD.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Say that again because I'm not sure if it got recorded. That was the first plane?

sp.speaker: Jack Lloyd
sp.p: The first plane crashed. And so fate was still on my side. Didn't make me feel any better, but that's the way things go. I got into Camp Lucky Strike and they have rows and rows of white tents, pup tents. In front of each row it would have a sign, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Iowa, New Jersey, New York. Whatever state you happened to be from, that's the row of tents that you went to, picked out a tent. Well, then they gave us a little miniphysical. They put a little metal tag around your neck and that was what you was supposed to--or get to--sort of a diet thing. They didn't tell us about it. They just put the tag around your neck and then left. I went into the mess line, had my canteen and my mess kit. The fellow put a little spoonful of rolled oats on my mess kit and put a little drop of jelly on it. He said, "Next." I said, "Wait, wait one second." I says, "I didn't come here to look at food, I want something to eat." Well, we got in quite an argument. And I wasn't the only one. Well, finally a sort of a miniriot broke out. Well, then the doctor got on a platform and he used one of those bullhorns explaining to us what these tags were. He said, "If they'd feed you more than what that tag says, you're liable to die because your stomach has been shrunk and so forth. Some worse than others." So they finally convinced us that was the way to go. We stayed there almost a month. They fed us like we were kings. We had ice cream, potatoes and chicken and gravy and they wanted to fatten us up a little bit so we didn't look so bad, I guess, when we got home, which was a good idea. Well, now, then, it's time to go home. Take me to a hospital ship. I walked up the plank. I got to a door, or a hatch, or whatever you call it. And they said, you go down three floors and that, they'll--they'll assign you a bunk. I said, "This is where we stop, I'm not going down. I'm--you guys liable to hit a dead mine that they hadn't retrieved and I'd be captured." I said, "I'm not going down there." Now, this holds up the line, got everybody a little ticked off. A doctor came past, must have had some compassion. He said, "If he don't want to go down there, tie a cot to the rail." And that's the way I came home. But I had somebody, they'd bring my food up. I wouldn't even go down. I--I was afraid. The ride home was just like sitting in a room at hop--at home. No waves, nothing. It was a big ship. Took us six days. But it was nice. The water was calm; the ride was good. We get into Boston. They had the people from the Red Cross down there, had a drum and some kind of a horn, somebody trying to sing. And we weren't impressed at all. With being--we didn't want that, we wanted to get off this ship and get home. Finally they took us off the ship. Well, just prior to getting off there was a fellow selling hotdogs in one of these stands that has two wheels on it. That's _____+. I told the fellow, I said, "I'm going down and get a hotdog." He said, "We're not allowed off--allowed off the ship." I said, "I don't care, I'm getting a hotdog." And down this gangplank I went. The two MPs were talking and I went in around behind them and started for the hotdog stand. And they hollered stop, or we'll shoot. I said, "Go ahead, I'm home." So I went over and I got a hotdog. And the fellow said that'd be ten or 15 cents. I don't recall which now. I said, "You're going to have to charge it because I don't any money." He said, "You from that ship?" Yep. He said, "Well, it's on the house." Well, he might as well have agreed with me because I didn't have it. Well, finally I get back on the ship. The MPs were a little put out about that, but that's the way it was. When it came to food I wasn't--wasn't gonna turn my back on any. Well, they finally left us off the ship and put us in a big warehouse. And I mean a big one. They had tables in lines. Must have had four lines of 'em in there. And in the one line you get clothes, in the next line you get your metals, and in another line they sewed the metals onto your jackets. I got in that line. I said, "I don't want mine on this new jacket, I'll keep them in that sack." No, you have to have them sewed on. I said, "You're not sewing them on my new uniform." So finally I guess I was holding up the line or they getting tired of it or something, but I got to keep them in a sack. So they gave me $2 and a train ticket to get home. I figured, well, if that's not enough at least I'm in the United States, I can make it home, no problem. Well, fortunately the train went on. Got off at New Castle, Pennsylvania. In the meantime, my dad and mother had moved, when I was in combat, and they sent me a picture of the house and the directions to get there. Well, I was pretty familiar with the area but I didn't know the house at all. So I walk into this bus station. I said, "When's the next bus going to Elwood?" They said, "This isn't a bus station, it's an electric company." I said, "When I left two years ago it was a bus station." Well, they said, "These fellows read meters, they aren't bus drivers. The bus station is about four blocks down the road." So I take my--they called it a barracks bag. And I threw it up over my shoulder and started to leave. He said, "Wait a minute." He said, "I have a fellow here who said he'll take you on down, that he's going that way anyhow." So I get in this fellow's car and we start down the road. But here he read my dad's meter, electric meter. That was his route. But he didn't tell me. He'd keep asking me, "Is this the house? Is that the house?" I'd keep saying no. He says, "How do you know?" I said, "Well, the Germans took all my stuff, wallets and pictures and everything. But," I said, "I think I'll remember." Well, finally after about ten houses I said, "Let's try that one up there." He said, "Are you sure?" And I said, "I said let's try it, it looks like what I remember." He didn't say it, but that was the house. We drove up the lane and got to the house. My smaller brother, now he was about nine years old. He was out playing in the backyard and he looks up and he saw me. I was still sittin' in the car. He jumps up and he runs for the house saying, "Jack's home, Jack's home." Well, my dad came to the door and he saw me. Instead of unlocking the screen door he walked right through it. Well, he came out. Then I said, "Where's
